title: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams
hook: a grammar teacher comes home from pilgrimage and every word he explains turns into Krishna

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramprasad, the clerk who wrote songs to Kali in his account book, cross with his Mother and hard on himself.

What happens to a grammar lesson when the teacher can only think of God? In Nabadwip, a town of scholars on the river, the teacher is young and sharp, known for his skill in Sanskrit grammar, and his students are proud to study with him. Then he goes away on a pilgrimage, and comes back different. He sits down to explain an ordinary word, a verb, a root, and somehow the explanation ends in Krishna. The next word, the same. The students look at each other. They came for grammar. Today, the Vaishnava stream, and a teacher you met earlier on this path: Chaitanya.
screen: `A YOUNG GRAMMAR TEACHER.` → `A PILGRIMAGE.` → `EVERY WORD ENDS IN KRISHNA.`

segments.voice: The biographies tell this story, and they don't make fun of the students. In the end he closes the school. He can't teach grammar anymore, because every word has become a door to the same room. So what does he do instead? He sings. With friends, in a courtyard at first, then out in the streets of Nabadwip: the names of God, Hari, Krishna, over and over to drums and cymbals, louder and faster, until people are dancing. That's kirtan, and in this stream it isn't decoration. It is the practice: the name, sung out loud, in company. The singing could sound like showing off. But Chaitanya is remembered for a handful of short teaching verses, and one of them, in paraphrase, says how to sing: humbler than a blade of grass, more patient than a tree, giving honor to others and wanting none for yourself. A tree, the old explanation goes, gives shade even to the one who cuts it down. So the loudest practice in the stream is meant to come from the lowest place. Remember the conch on Bengal's first day, the Goddess as Mother? The Vaishnava stream also reaches for a close name. For Chaitanya's followers the closest of all is Radha's love for Krishna, and in their stories Chaitanya himself weeps and longs for Krishna the way Radha does. The scholar who couldn't stop saying Krishna ends up singing in the street, as low as grass.
screen: `EVERY WORD BECOMES KRISHNA` · `THE NAME, SUNG IN THE STREETS` · `HUMBLER THAN A BLADE OF GRASS` · `LONGING LIKE RADHA`

segments.voice: On the in-breath, picture a blade of grass, low, bending when it's walked on, standing up again; on the out-breath, a tree, rooted, patient, giving shade. Go back and forth, grass and tree, and bring to mind one person who might need you to bend, or to wait. If you pray, let a name of God, Hari or Krishna or your own, sound softly with the breath.
Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams: the Vaishnava stream in Chaitanya, the grammar teacher who sang the names of Krishna in the street, humbler than a blade of grass. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams. Every word, a door to the same room. Until tomorrow.

notes: Editor pass: hook opener changed (several Bengal hooks opened 'A [place]...'); light wording change in the teach.

The pilgrimage is to Gaya in the biographies; the script leaves it unnamed. Confirm the story of his grammar teaching turning to Krishna and the closing of his school (Chaitanya Bhagavata, Madhya-khanda).

Shikshashtakam 3 paraphrased (trinad api sunichena, taror iva sahishnuna, amanina manadena, kirtaniyah sada harih). The tree giving shade even to the one who cuts it is from the traditional commentary (e.g. Chaitanya Charitamrita Antya 20); confirm.
Chaitanya's absorption in Radha's mood is stated as what his followers' stories say. Gaudiya theology holds Chaitanya to be Radha and Krishna combined; deliberately not stated. A Keeper may want it.
The Kazi episode was deliberately not used, to avoid casting another tradition as an obstacle.
